### I. The Science of Vanishing Places

The city of Sulis was not built upon rock, clay, or silt, though if you dug beneath the cellar flagstones of the Old Library, you would find soil dark enough to stain your fingernails for a week. Sulis was built upon attention.

When the citizens of Sulis turned their backs upon an alleyway—when no lover paused beneath its gas lamps, when no coal cart rattled down its cobbles, when even the alley cat found a warmer wall against which to curl its ribs—the alleyway began to thin. First, the mortar between the bricks would soften into a fine, gray meal, like dried flour. Then the shadows would lose their sharpness, smudging at the edges until the darkness beneath the stairwells looked less like shade and more like spilled soot. Finally, usually between three and four in the morning when the collective sleep of the city was at its deepest, the space would simply pull itself together like an accordioned sleeve. Two buildings that had been separated by twelve feet of damp limestone would wake up pressed cheek-to-cheek, their plaster molding touching, leaving no seam, no scar, and no memory of the passage that had been between them.

My name is Julian, and I am a Surveyor of the Third Bureau. It is my duty to measure that which is about to disappear.

I carry my tools in a brass-bound box of dark walnut that sloshes slightly when I walk, owing to the three bottles of iron-gall ink suspended in oil at its center. I have a pair of brass dividers whose points are tipped with obsidian; a thirty-foot ribbon of woven silk impregnated with lead dust so that it lays flat against uneven pavement; and a heavy, brass-cased chronometer that does not measure hours, but rather the rate at which sound decays in a given room.

When a room is about to fade, it grows quiet in a way that has nothing to do with silence. A normal silent room holds the echo of your breath, the scrape of your boot heel, the small, dry click of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. A fading room absorbs these things without returning them. You can clap your hands in a fading drawing room and the sound will drop to the floor like a dead sparrow, flat and heavy, leaving no ripple in the air.

This morning, the Bureau sent me to the District of the Weavers.

The Weavers’ Quarter had been shrinking for thirty years, ever since the mechanical looms were introduced across the river in New St. Jude. The mechanical looms did not require human hands to guide the shuttles, nor did they require the old wooden houses with their tall, north-facing windows where three generations of thread-spinners used to live, sleep, and spit into the hearth. As the weavers died or moved toward the soot-choked iron yards of the south, their neighborhood shrank like a wet leather glove left out in the sun.

I stood at the corner of Threadneedle Street and the Passage of St. Roch. According to the map drawn by my predecessor seventy years ago, Threadneedle Street possessed forty-two chimneys, six public pumps, and a tavern called *The Black Shuttle*.

I looked up the street. I counted nine chimneys.

The street was now so narrow that two men carrying umbrellas could not pass one another without tilting their frames. The upper stories of the houses leaned together like old gossips sharing a toothless secret, their gables almost locking fingers across the strip of pale, gray sky above.

"You're late," said a voice from a doorway.

It was Master Vane. He was eighty-one years old, though his skin had taken on the yellowed, translucent quality of oiled parchment, making him look as though he might be older than the street itself—or perhaps made of the same materials. He was the last loom-maker in the quarter.

"The tram was delayed at the river," I said, setting my walnut box down upon a doorframe that was already cold—not cold with the chill of winter, but cold with the absence of purpose. "The bridge lost three yards during the night."

Vane spat onto the cobbles. His saliva was clear and thin. "They don't maintain the piers. They think because everyone takes the steam launch now, the bridge can take care of itself. A bridge needs boots on it, Julian. A bridge that isn't walked on forgets how to hold its own weight."

"Is the workshop still here?" I asked.

"Half of it," he said, stepping back to let me pass. "The back pantry went on Tuesday. I kept my beechwood templates in there. Sixty years of shuttle-shapes. Gone between the time I put the kettle on and the time it boiled. Didn't even hear a rustle."

I stepped into the hallway. The air smelled of old linseed oil, dry oak dust, and the peculiar, ozone-sharp tang that precedes a collapse. I drew my ribbon of lead-weighted silk from my box and handed one end to Vane.

"Hold this against the skirting board," I said. "And do not let go, no matter what you hear."

***

### II. The Geometry of Forgetting

To understand Sulis, one must understand that a map is not a record of what exists; it is an argument against non-existence.

When I lay my leaded silk along the floorboards of Master Vane’s workshop, I am not merely measuring twelve feet and four inches of pine. I am scribing those twelve feet into the official register at the Central Atrium. So long as the ink remains wet upon my ledger, the floorboards have a legal and physical tether to the earth. They cannot shrink smaller than the numbers written in my book without creating a discrepancy in the Municipal Tax Register, and if there is one thing the architecture of Sulis fears more than human indifference, it is an unregistered ledger entry.

"Twelve feet, four inches," I muttered, dipping my nib into the iron-gall.

The point of the steel pen scratched across the heavy rag paper. The sound was loud in the small room—too loud. The walls were already swallowing the room's ambient resonance, leaving only the sharp, needle-like sound of my writing.

"It's moving faster today," Vane said. His voice sounded thin, as if he were speaking through a wool blanket.

"Where is the window?" I asked, looking up.

The north wall had six panels of glass when I visited three months ago. Now there were four. The two eastern panes had simply vanished, and the pine frame had drawn itself together, closing the gap so smoothly that the grain of the wood ran straight through the joint without a scar or a knot to show where the wood had been worked.

"It happened while I was sleeping," Vane said. He reached into his waistcoat pocket and pulled out a small, wooden object—a shuttle, carved from dark boxwood, its metal tips polished bright by forty years of thumb-grease. "I held onto this. I thought if I held onto something small, the room would remember the rest of it."

"It doesn't work that way, Master Vane," I said gently. "The object must be shared. A private memory is too light. It lacks the weight to hold down a ceiling."

"My wife died in that corner," he said, pointing to a spot near the hearth where the floorboards were distinctly darker, stained by years of spilled tea and wet firewood. "She died there in ninety-four. She had a blue shawl with silver fringe. I can still tell you the number of picks per inch in that weave. Forty-eight. Two-ply silk warp, combed wool weft. You tell me that corner doesn't have weight?"

I looked at the corner. The shadow there was not black; it was a dull, flat slate-gray. The mop-board had already separated from the plaster by half an inch, exposing not the lath behind it, but a gray, featureless void that looked like compressed fog.

"The corner will be gone by nightfall," I said. "You must pack your irons and your small tools. The Bureau has assigned you a room on the third floor of the Pensioners' Row in New St. Jude."

Vane looked at me with his pale, watery eyes. "There are no windows in the Pensioners' Row that look at the river."

"No," I admitted. "They look at the gasworks."

"And the floors there," he continued, "they are made of poured concrete. You can't hear a man walking on concrete. You can't tell if he’s coming toward you or going away."

"Concrete doesn't shrink," I said. It was the only comfort I could offer him. It was a cold comfort, carved from the same utilitarian stone as the pensions themselves. Concrete was indifferent to memory. It was mixed with gravel from the high quarries where no one had ever lived, stirred by steam power, and laid down in long, lifeless slabs that neither expanded with love nor withered with neglect. It was permanent because it was dead.

I unclasped my dividers and measured the distance between the hearth and the door. Nine feet.

Three weeks ago, it had been fourteen.

"Leave the heavy lathe," I told him. "You won't be able to get it through the door by afternoon. The frame is already six inches narrower than it was when I arrived."

Vane did not answer. He sat down on a three-legged stool near the diminishing window, placed his boxwood shuttle on his knee, and began to rub its smooth wooden flank with his calloused thumb. *Scratch. Scratch. Scratch.*

The sound was the only thing left in the room that had an echo.

***

### III. The Central Atrium and the Great Ledger

I returned to the Third Bureau at four in the afternoon.

The Bureau was housed in the basement of the High Court, a building so vast and heavily frequented that it had not lost an inch of its perimeter since the reign of the First Council. Its granite steps were hollowed out by two hundred years of leather soles, and its corridors smelled of wet wool, tobacco smoke, and the stale vinegar used by the cleaners to scrub the ink-stains off the marble window ledges.

Here, the air was dense and heavy. Sounds bounced off the vaulted stone ceilings with a metallic clatter—the ringing of brass call-bells, the heavy *thump* of leather registers being dropped onto oak desks, the wet click of brass pneumatic tubes swallowing metal canisters.

I walked down Corridor C to the Registry of Shrinkage.

Director Mara was sitting behind her double-sloped desk, a pair of green glass spectacles resting on the bridge of her flat nose. She was sixty, perhaps seventy, with hair the color of salt-cured cod and fingers that were permanently stained purple from copy-ink.

"The Weavers' Quarter?" she asked without looking up from her ledger.

"Threadneedle Street," I said, setting my walnut box on the floor and handing her my field book. "Numbers fourteen through twenty-eight are gone. Number twelve will be gone by morning. Master Vane is being relocated to the Pensioners' Row."

Mara took the field book and ran her ink-stained index finger down my column of figures. She stopped at the bottom.

"You've recorded nine feet between the hearth and the door at Number Twelve," she said.

"Yes, Director."

"The Municipal Index of 1840 records twenty-two feet."

"The Municipal Index is eighty years old," I said. "The street has lost twelve houses since then. The density of attention has dropped below the critical threshold. There are only four people left living on the entire block, and three of them are blind."

Mara sighed, a small, wheezing sound that smelled faintly of peppermint lozenges. She pulled a heavy brass stamp from its stand, pressed it against a ink-pad soaked in purple dye, and brought it down on my field notes with a sharp *clack*.

*CANCELLED.*

"The Great Map must be adjusted," she said. "Take the lift to the Third Sub-level. Tell the draftsman that Threadneedle Street is now an unpaved lane of ninety yards."

"It isn't ninety yards," I said softly. "It's barely sixty."

"It is ninety yards on the master grid until the end of the quarter," she replied, her glass spectacles reflecting the blue flame of the gas burner behind her head. "If we shrink it too fast on the map, the gas mains beneath the street will buckle. We have to draw the lines shorter by degrees, Julian. Give the iron pipes time to settle into the soil. If we pull the city together faster than the ground can collapse, we get air pockets. And you know what happens when we get air pockets."

I knew. Six years ago, the Old Fish Market had vanished in a single night because the fishmongers had all moved to the cold-storage plant by the docks. The Bureau had failed to update the ledgers in time. A void three hundred feet wide had opened beneath the pavement, and two milk wagons, a street lamp, and a night-watchman had fallen into a cellar that had technically ceased to exist three days prior. They had never found the watchman. When they dug into the earth where the market had been, they found only solid, undisturbed gravel, as if no shovel had ever breached the soil since the time of the Romans.

"How is Mara's Lane?" I asked.

The Director paused, her hand hovering over a fresh stack of linen-backed ledger sheets. For a second—just a second—the hard, bureaucratic set of her jaw softened.

"My lane," she said, "is two yards wide today. My sister's garden bench is half in the kitchen and half in the fence."

"Are you moving her?"

"She won't move," Mara said. "She says the soil in New St. Jude is sour. She says if she can't smell her lavender, she doesn't care whether her feet are inside the house or out of it."

She dipped her pen again. "Go down to the Draftsmen, Julian. And take your oil bottle. The counter-weights in the lift were squeaking this morning."

***

### IV. The House That Remembers

I did not go directly to the Third Sub-level.

Instead, I took my walnut box and stepped out through the rear archway of the High Court, into the small, triangular courtyard known as the Garden of the Archons.

It was not a real garden. There were no trees, no flowers, and no grass. It was merely a wedge of space trapped between three immense administrative buildings, paved with flagstones that were turned twice a year to keep the moss from gaining a hold. In the center of the courtyard sat a stone fountain that had not run with water since the great drought of '08.

Sitting on the edge of the dry basin was a woman I had seen three times this month.

She was young—perhaps twenty-five—and she wore a high-collared coat of dark green wool that had been mended at the cuffs with thread that didn't quite match. She had a sketchbook open on her knee, and she was drawing with a piece of soft willow charcoal that made a dry *hissing* sound as she moved her hand.

I walked over and stood behind her, keeping my shadow off her paper.

She was not drawing the fountain, nor was she drawing the massive stone facade of the Ministry of Taxes behind it. She was drawing a door.

It was an arched door, made of heavy oak planks studded with square-headed iron nails. Above the door was a transom of carved stone depicting a fox running through a field of rye.

"There is no door like that in this courtyard," I said.

She did not look up, but her charcoal paused for a fraction of a second against the paper. "There was," she said.

"When?"

"Forty years ago," she said. "My grandfather had a saddlery here. Before they built the High Court Annex. The door was right where that iron drain-pipe comes down from the roof."

"The Annex was built in '82," I said. "The saddlery was demolished."

"It wasn't demolished," she said, finally turning her head to look at me. Her eyes were very clear, a strange, pale hazel that seemed to catch the gray northern light of the courtyard. "They built the stone wall around it. They didn't tear the house down; they just stopped letting people go through the door. My grandfather stayed inside for three days while the masons were laying the ashlar blocks across the entry."

"That's impossible," I said, though my voice lacked conviction. I was a Surveyor; I knew the limits of space in Sulis better than anyone. "He would have been smothered. There's three feet of solid granite behind that pipe."

"He had six barrels of salted herring," she said, turning back to her sketchbook. "And twelve gallons of cider. And he had forty years of horse-collars to sew."

She reached out with her pinky finger and smudged the shadow beneath the carved stone fox.

"Do you know why I come here every Thursday, Surveyor?" she asked.

"To draw," I said.

"I come here to look at the drain-pipe," she said. "Because every Thursday at three o'clock, I can smell tan-bark. Dry oak bark and grease. If I stop drawing the door, the smell goes away."

I reached into my box and took out my brass dividers. I opened them to six inches and placed the obsidian points against the granite wall behind the drain-pipe.

I brought my ear close to the cold stone.

In a normal wall, you hear nothing except the high, distant hum of the city's traffic transferred through the earth—the rumble of drays three blocks away, the thump of the steam presses at the newspaper office, the deep, rhythmic *throb* of the river pumps.

Against this wall, I heard something else.

It was very small, very dry, and very regular.

*Thump. Stitch. Pull.*

*Thump. Stitch. Pull.*

The sound of an awl punching through heavy harness-leather, followed by the dry whistle of a waxed linen thread being drawn tight by two scarred hands.

"He's eighty-six now," the girl said softly. "In there."

"He can't be," I whispered. "It's been forty years. He would have run out of salt herring in six months."

"Time doesn't move at twelve inches to the foot in a closed space," she said. She closed her sketchbook with a soft *snap* that sent a tiny cloud of charcoal dust into the cold air. "If you don't let any light in, the room doesn't know what year it is. It just stays whatever Tuesday it was when you laid the last brick."

I stood up, my knees cracking like dry twigs. My hands were trembling slightly as I replaced the dividers in their walnut groove.

"What is your name?" I asked.

"Eleni," she said.

"Eleni, you must not draw this door anymore."

She looked up at me, her hazel eyes squinting against the gray glare of the clouds. "Why? Because it isn't in your book?"

"Because if you draw it too well," I said, "the wall will become thin. The High Court weighs six thousand tons, Eleni. If the stone behind that pipe loses its thickness because you're remembering a saddlery that isn't there, the entire south wing will settle into the void. Three hundred clerks will fall through the floor into three feet of salted herring bones and horse-grease."

She laughed. It was a clear, ringing sound—a bright, silver bell struck in a vault full of wool.

For a moment—just the briefest fraction of a second—the gray stone of the wall behind her seemed to flicker. The gray granite turned the color of dry oak timber, and for six feet around her head, the air smelled so strongly of birch-tar and leather grease that my nostrils twitched.

Then she stood up, tucked her sketchbook under her arm, and walked away toward the iron gates.

The smell of leather vanished instantly, replaced by the damp, sour odor of cold cabbage from the basement kitchens of the High Court.

***

### V. The Map of the Unseen

That night, I did not sleep in my room at the Surveyors' Barracks.

I stayed late in the Third Sub-level, long after the draftsmen had put away their T-squares and turned off their gas jets. The Great Map lay across four long oak tables joined together with iron clamps. It was twelve feet long and eight feet wide, drawn on three-ply vellum made from the skins of sheep that had grazed on the high pastures before the foundation of the city.

The ink was black, green, red, and blue.

The black lines were roads that had been measured three times by three separate surveyors.

The green lines were parks and gardens—though most of these had been pinched down to small, olive-colored splatters no larger than a postage stamp.

The red lines were public buildings: the High Court, the Mint, the Granary, the Prison.

And the blue lines—the blue lines were the ghosts.

They were drawn in pale ultramarine ink that had been diluted with vinegar so that it would fade after twenty years. The blue lines represented the streets that were in *transition*—the places that were being forgotten, but had not yet completely drawn their shoulders together and vanished into the soil.

I stood over the table with a bottle of blue ink and a fine crow-quill pen.

I found the square marked *The District of the Weavers*.

Threadneedle Street was there, a thin, crooked blue worm crawling between the thick red block of the Steam Loom Works and the black line of the River Sulis.

I dipped my pen.

I ought to have drawn a red cross through Numbers Fourteen through Twenty-Eight. I ought to have taken my razor and scraped away the small blue square that marked Master Vane’s workshop, leaving only the clean, cream-colored surface of the blank vellum to show where the land had become empty and void.

That was the rule. That was the Science of the Third Bureau.

*We do not create,* the oath said. *We only subtract.*

I looked at the blue square of Number Twelve.

I remembered the boxwood shuttle. I remembered the forty-eight picks per inch of blue silk warp and wool weft. I remembered the dry, scratchy sound of Master Vane’s thumb rubbing the polished wood while his floorboards shrank around him like a dying leaf.

I did not scrape the vellum.

Instead, I set my crow-quill down and picked up a tiny camel-hair brush—the kind used by the illuminators who decorated the ornamental borders of the Municipal Charters.

I dipped the tip into the blue ink. Then I dipped it into a saucer of clear water, diluting the blue until it was as pale as the eye of an old weaver.

Very carefully, with a hand that had been trained to measure sixty-fourths of an inch by the feel of a screw-thread, I began to draw.

I did not shrink Threadneedle Street.

I widened it.

I drew three new houses behind Master Vane’s lathe-room. I gave them narrow gardens with pear trees against the stone walls. I drew a small lane—a lane that had never existed on any map since the foundation of the city—leading from the back of the loom-works down to the mud-flats of the river.

I called it *Shuttle Lane*.

I gave it six gas lamps. I gave it a pub called *The Weaver’s Rest*. I gave it a small, stone trough where horses could drink cold river water while their drivers unloaded the crates of raw wool.

As I painted the last faint blue line of the watering trough, I felt a strange, cold vibration in the wood of the drawing table beneath my wrists.

It was not a tremor of the earth. It was a shift in the *tension* of the building.

Somewhere three floors above me, in the long, dark corridors of the High Court, a floorboard gave a loud, dry *CRACK*.

It was the sound of a joist expanding. It was the sound of timber remembering that it had once been forty feet long instead of thirty-six.

I held my breath.

The sound did not repeat. But when I leaned down and brought my nose close to the fresh blue ink on the vellum, the smell of vinegar and iron-gall was gone.

In its place was the smell of damp river mud, wet pear leaves, and the sharp, warm scent of wool grease coming off a newly filled shuttle.

***

### VI. The Threshold

At six in the morning, the night-watchman found me sleeping with my head upon the table, my cheek resting against the western edge of the Great Map.

"Julian," he said, shaking my shoulder with a hand that smelled of plug-tobacco and brass polish. "Wake up, lad. The Director's coming down the stairs."

I sat up, my neck stiff, my mouth tasting of zinc and cold tea.

The blue ink had dried.

*Shuttle Lane* was still there. It did not look like an addition; the pale blue ink had sunk into the old sheepskin, blending with the sixty-year-old lines drawn by long-dead surveyors until you could not tell where the old city ended and my lie began.

I packed my brass tools into my walnut box—the dividers, the leaded silk, the obsidian points, the iron-gall ink.

I did not wait for Director Mara to reach the sub-level. I took the narrow spiral stairs that led up to the delivery yard behind the kitchens, where the coal carts were already backing in through the fog.

The air outside was freezing. A low, river-born mist had crept over the granite walls during the night, wrapping the street lamp posts in thick, yellow scarves of moisture.

I walked north.

I did not take the tram. I did not take the new iron bridge. I walked through the small, twisting alleyways that were not supposed to be there anymore—the ones that had been marked for cancellation five years ago, but somehow still hung on between the backs of the soap factories and the timber yards.

I reached the District of the Weavers at seven.

The fog was so thick here that I could only see ten feet in front of my boots. The silence was absolute—no cart wheels, no milk-bells, no shouting of newsboys.

I turned the corner where Threadneedle Street was supposed to end.

According to my field book from yesterday, I should have found a blank brick wall belonging to the Steam Loom Works, pressed tight against the side of Master Vane’s house.

I did not find a wall.

I found an opening.

It was a narrow lane, paved with rough river cobbles that were bright with wet moss. On the left side stood three small, timber-framed houses with steep gables and north-facing windows. In the garden of the middle house, a pear tree—stunted and gray with river-mist—lifted its bare, crooked branches toward the sky.

A man was standing at the corner beneath a brass gas lamp that flickered with a small, yellow tongue of flame.

He wore a green coat with mended cuffs, and he was holding a brass key that was six inches long.

"You're early, Surveyor," Master Vane said.

He was not carrying his boxwood shuttle. He didn't need to. It was tucked into his waistcoat pocket, its bright brass tip showing above the leather lip like the beak of a small, sleeping bird.

"Where does this lane go?" I asked, my voice soundless in the damp air.

Vane looked down the lane. The fog was beginning to lift, just enough to show the long, gray curve of the cobbles as they dipped down toward the river.

"It goes to the water," he said. "There's a wharf at the end. A small one. Enough for two barges of timber."

"It wasn't here yesterday," I said.

Vane smiled. His teeth were yellow and few, but his eyes were bright—brighter than they had been in his narrow room with the four glass panes.

"It's been here seventy years, Julian," he said. "We just forgot to open the door."

He turned and walked down the lane, his boots making a crisp, heavy *clack-clack-clack* against the cobbles. It was a good sound. It was the sound of a man who weighed one hundred and sixty pounds, walking on stone that had five feet of solid earth beneath it.

I did not follow him.

I set my walnut box down on the curb at the entrance to Shuttle Lane.

I unclasped the brass latches. I took out my field book—the one filled with columns of figures, purple *CANCELLED* stamps, and measurements of rooms that had shrunk to nothing.

I opened it to the first page.

I took my obsidian-tipped dividers and I drove them straight through the thick rag paper, through the leather cover, and deep into the wet wood of the walnut box itself, locking them together in a single, unyielding cross.

Then I left the box sitting on the cobbles beneath the gas lamp.

I walked back toward the city—not by the High Court, not by the Bureau, and not by the great stone avenues that had been measured by iron chains.

I walked through the spaces between the lines.

I found an alley where the gas lamps were out. I found a yard where three old men were playing bowls in the gray light, using wooden balls that had been turned on lathes that were demolished in '92. I found a tea-house that sat in the middle of a street that the Great Map said was six feet wide.

The tea-house was three stories high, and its windows were lit with small, warm tallow candles that smelled of mutton fat and cinnamon.

I went inside.

I sat down at a small marble table near the hearth. The floorboards were pine, seven inches wide, with knots that looked like dark, open eyes.

A girl came to my table. She carried a heavy tin pot and two white stoneware cups.

"Are you the new surveyor?" she asked.

"No," I said, reaching into my coat pocket and finding two copper coins that were so worn they had lost the face of the King. "I am the man who lost the tape measure."

She poured the tea. It was dark, hot, and smelled of wood-smoke.

Outside the window, I heard the sound of the city—not the city of iron and concrete, not the city that shrank every night at four in the morning, but the city that lives under the charcoal drawings of girls with hazel eyes.

It was very wide. It was very long. And as far as I could hear through the clear, winter air, it had no walls at all.

"Is the workshop still here?" I asked.

"Half of it," he said, stepping back to let me pass. "The back pantry went on Tuesday. I kept my beechwood templates in there. Sixty years of shuttle-shapes. Gone between the time I put the kettle on and the time it boiled. Didn't even hear a rustle."

I stepped into the hallway. The air smelled of old linseed oil, dry oak dust, and the peculiar, ozone-sharp tang that precedes a collapse. I drew my ribbon of lead-weighted silk from my box and handed one end to Vane.

"Hold this against the skirting board," I said. "And do not let go, no matter what you hear."

***

### II. The Geometry of Forgetting

To understand Sulis, one must understand that a map is not a record of what exists; it is an argument against non-existence.

When I lay my leaded silk along the floorboards of Master Vane’s workshop, I am not merely measuring twelve feet and four inches of pine. I am scribing those twelve feet into the official register at the Central Atrium. So long as the ink remains wet upon my ledger, the floorboards have a legal and physical tether to the earth. They cannot shrink smaller than the numbers written in my book without creating a discrepancy in the Municipal Tax Register, and if there is one thing the architecture of Sulis fears more than human indifference, it is an unregistered ledger entry.

"Twelve feet, four inches," I muttered, dipping my nib into the iron-gall.

The point of the steel pen scratched across the heavy rag paper. The sound was loud in the small room—too loud. The walls were already swallowing the room's ambient resonance, leaving only the sharp, needle-like sound of my writing.

"It's moving faster today," Vane said. His voice sounded thin, as if he were speaking through a wool blanket.

"Where is the window?" I asked, looking up.

The north wall had six panels of glass when I visited three months ago. Now there were four. The two eastern panes had simply vanished, and the pine frame had drawn itself together, closing the gap so smoothly that the grain of the wood ran straight through the joint without a scar or a knot to show where the wood had been worked.

"It happened while I was sleeping," Vane said. He reached into his waistcoat pocket and pulled out a small, wooden object—a shuttle, carved from dark boxwood, its metal tips polished bright by forty years of thumb-grease. "I held onto this. I thought if I held onto something small, the room would remember the rest of it."

"It doesn't work that way, Master Vane," I said gently. "The object must be shared. A private memory is too light. It lacks the weight to hold down a ceiling."

"My wife died in that corner," he said, pointing to a spot near the hearth where the floorboards were distinctly darker, stained by years of spilled tea and wet firewood. "She died there in ninety-four. She had a blue shawl with silver fringe. I can still tell you the number of picks per inch in that weave. Forty-eight. Two-ply silk warp, combed wool weft. You tell me that corner doesn't have weight?"

I looked at the corner. The shadow there was not black; it was a dull, flat slate-gray. The mop-board had already separated from the plaster by half an inch, exposing not the lath behind it, but a gray, featureless void that looked like compressed fog.

"The corner will be gone by nightfall," I said. "You must pack your irons and your small tools. The Bureau has assigned you a room on the third floor of the Pensioners' Row in New St. Jude."

Vane looked at me with his pale, watery eyes. "There are no windows in the Pensioners' Row that look at the river."

"No," I admitted. "They look at the gasworks."

"And the floors there," he continued, "they are made of poured concrete. You can't hear a man walking on concrete. You can't tell if he’s coming toward you or going away."

"Concrete doesn't shrink," I said. It was the only comfort I could offer him. It was a cold comfort, carved from the same utilitarian stone as the pensions themselves. Concrete was indifferent to memory. It was mixed with gravel from the high quarries where no one had ever lived, stirred by steam power, and laid down in long, lifeless slabs that neither expanded with love nor withered with neglect. It was permanent because it was dead.

I unclasped my dividers and measured the distance between the hearth and the door. Nine feet.

Three weeks ago, it had been fourteen.

"Leave the heavy lathe," I told him. "You won't be able to get it through the door by afternoon. The frame is already six inches narrower than it was when I arrived."

Vane did not answer. He sat down on a three-legged stool near the diminishing window, placed his boxwood shuttle on his knee, and began to rub its smooth wooden flank with his calloused thumb. *Scratch. Scratch. Scratch.*

The sound was the only thing left in the room that had an echo.

***

### III. The Central Atrium and the Great Ledger

I returned to the Third Bureau at four in the afternoon.

The Bureau was housed in the basement of the High Court, a building so vast and heavily frequented that it had not lost an inch of its perimeter since the reign of the First Council. Its granite steps were hollowed out by two hundred years of leather soles, and its corridors smelled of wet wool, tobacco smoke, and the stale vinegar used by the cleaners to scrub the ink-stains off the marble window ledges.

Here, the air was dense and heavy. Sounds bounced off the vaulted stone ceilings with a metallic clatter—the ringing of brass call-bells, the heavy *thump* of leather registers being dropped onto oak desks, the wet click of brass pneumatic tubes swallowing metal canisters.

I walked down Corridor C to the Registry of Shrinkage.

Director Mara was sitting behind her double-sloped desk, a pair of green glass spectacles resting on the bridge of her flat nose. She was sixty, perhaps seventy, with hair the color of salt-cured cod and fingers that were permanently stained purple from copy-ink.

"The Weavers' Quarter?" she asked without looking up from her ledger.

"Threadneedle Street," I said, setting my walnut box on the floor and handing her my field book. "Numbers fourteen through twenty-eight are gone. Number twelve will be gone by morning. Master Vane is being relocated to the Pensioners' Row."

Mara took the field book and ran her ink-stained index finger down my column of figures. She stopped at the bottom.

"You've recorded nine feet between the hearth and the door at Number Twelve," she said.

"Yes, Director."

"The Municipal Index of 1840 records twenty-two feet."

"The Municipal Index is eighty years old," I said. "The street has lost twelve houses since then. The density of attention has dropped below the critical threshold. There are only four people left living on the entire block, and three of them are blind."

Mara sighed, a small, wheezing sound that smelled faintly of peppermint lozenges. She pulled a heavy brass stamp from its stand, pressed it against a ink-pad soaked in purple dye, and brought it down on my field notes with a sharp *clack*.

*CANCELLED.*

"The Great Map must be adjusted," she said. "Take the lift to the Third Sub-level. Tell the draftsman that Threadneedle Street is now an unpaved lane of ninety yards."

"It isn't ninety yards," I said softly. "It's barely sixty."

"It is ninety yards on the master grid until the end of the quarter," she replied, her glass spectacles reflecting the blue flame of the gas burner behind her head. "If we shrink it too fast on the map, the gas mains beneath the street will buckle. We have to draw the lines shorter by degrees, Julian. Give the iron pipes time to settle into the soil. If we pull the city together faster than the ground can collapse, we get air pockets. And you know what happens when we get air pockets."

I knew. Six years ago, the Old Fish Market had vanished in a single night because the fishmongers had all moved to the cold-storage plant by the docks. The Bureau had failed to update the ledgers in time. A void three hundred feet wide had opened beneath the pavement, and two milk wagons, a street lamp, and a night-watchman had fallen into a cellar that had technically ceased to exist three days prior. They had never found the watchman. When they dug into the earth where the market had been, they found only solid, undisturbed gravel, as if no shovel had ever breached the soil since the time of the Romans.

"How is Mara's Lane?" I asked.

The Director paused, her hand hovering over a fresh stack of linen-backed ledger sheets. For a second—just a second—the hard, bureaucratic set of her jaw softened.

"My lane," she said, "is two yards wide today. My sister's garden bench is half in the kitchen and half in the fence."

"Are you moving her?"

"She won't move," Mara said. "She says the soil in New St. Jude is sour. She says if she can't smell her lavender, she doesn't care whether her feet are inside the house or out of it."

She dipped her pen again. "Go down to the Draftsmen, Julian. And take your oil bottle. The counter-weights in the lift were squeaking this morning."

***

### IV. The House That Remembers

I did not go directly to the Third Sub-level.

Instead, I took my walnut box and stepped out through the rear archway of the High Court, into the small, triangular courtyard known as the Garden of the Archons.

It was not a real garden. There were no trees, no flowers, and no grass. It was merely a wedge of space trapped between three immense administrative buildings, paved with flagstones that were turned twice a year to keep the moss from gaining a hold. In the center of the courtyard sat a stone fountain that had not run with water since the great drought of '08.

Sitting on the edge of the dry basin was a woman I had seen three times this month.

She was young—perhaps twenty-five—and she wore a high-collared coat of dark green wool that had been mended at the cuffs with thread that didn't quite match. She had a sketchbook open on her knee, and she was drawing with a piece of soft willow charcoal that made a dry *hissing* sound as she moved her hand.

I walked over and stood behind her, keeping my shadow off her paper.

She was not drawing the fountain, nor was she drawing the massive stone facade of the Ministry of Taxes behind it. She was drawing a door.

It was an arched door, made of heavy oak planks studded with square-headed iron nails. Above the door was a transom of carved stone depicting a fox running through a field of rye.

"There is no door like that in this courtyard," I said.

She did not look up, but her charcoal paused for a fraction of a second against the paper. "There was," she said.

"When?"

"Forty years ago," she said. "My grandfather had a saddlery here. Before they built the High Court Annex. The door was right where that iron drain-pipe comes down from the roof."

"The Annex was built in '82," I said. "The saddlery was demolished."

"It wasn't demolished," she said, finally turning her head to look at me. Her eyes were very clear, a strange, pale hazel that seemed to catch the gray northern light of the courtyard. "They built the stone wall around it. They didn't tear the house down; they just stopped letting people go through the door. My grandfather stayed inside for three days while the masons were laying the ashlar blocks across the entry."

"That's impossible," I said, though my voice lacked conviction. I was a Surveyor; I knew the limits of space in Sulis better than anyone. "He would have been smothered. There's three feet of solid granite behind that pipe."

"He had six barrels of salted herring," she said, turning back to her sketchbook. "And twelve gallons of cider. And he had forty years of horse-collars to sew."

She reached out with her pinky finger and smudged the shadow beneath the carved stone fox.

"Do you know why I come here every Thursday, Surveyor?" she asked.

"To draw," I said.

"I come here to look at the drain-pipe," she said. "Because every Thursday at three o'clock, I can smell tan-bark. Dry oak bark and grease. If I stop drawing the door, the smell goes away."

I reached into my box and took out my brass dividers. I opened them to six inches and placed the obsidian points against the granite wall behind the drain-pipe.

I brought my ear close to the cold stone.

In a normal wall, you hear nothing except the high, distant hum of the city's traffic transferred through the earth—the rumble of drays three blocks away, the thump of the steam presses at the newspaper office, the deep, rhythmic *throb* of the river pumps.

Against this wall, I heard something else.

It was very small, very dry, and very regular.

*Thump. Stitch. Pull.*

*Thump. Stitch. Pull.*

The sound of an awl punching through heavy harness-leather, followed by the dry whistle of a waxed linen thread being drawn tight by two scarred hands.

"He's eighty-six now," the girl said softly. "In there."

"He can't be," I whispered. "It's been forty years. He would have run out of salt herring in six months."

"Time doesn't move at twelve inches to the foot in a closed space," she said. She closed her sketchbook with a soft *snap* that sent a tiny cloud of charcoal dust into the cold air. "If you don't let any light in, the room doesn't know what year it is. It just stays whatever Tuesday it was when you laid the last brick."

I stood up, my knees cracking like dry twigs. My hands were trembling slightly as I replaced the dividers in their walnut groove.

"What is your name?" I asked.

"Eleni," she said.

"Eleni, you must not draw this door anymore."

She looked up at me, her hazel eyes squinting against the gray glare of the clouds. "Why? Because it isn't in your book?"

"Because if you draw it too well," I said, "the wall will become thin. The High Court weighs six thousand tons, Eleni. If the stone behind that pipe loses its thickness because you're remembering a saddlery that isn't there, the entire south wing will settle into the void. Three hundred clerks will fall through the floor into three feet of salted herring bones and horse-grease."

She laughed. It was a clear, ringing sound—a bright, silver bell struck in a vault full of wool.

For a moment—just the briefest fraction of a second—the gray stone of the wall behind her seemed to flicker. The gray granite turned the color of dry oak timber, and for six feet around her head, the air smelled so strongly of birch-tar and leather grease that my nostrils twitched.

Then she stood up, tucked her sketchbook under her arm, and walked away toward the iron gates.

The smell of leather vanished instantly, replaced by the damp, sour odor of cold cabbage from the basement kitchens of the High Court.

***

### V. The Map of the Unseen

That night, I did not sleep in my room at the Surveyors' Barracks.

I stayed late in the Third Sub-level, long after the draftsmen had put away their T-squares and turned off their gas jets. The Great Map lay across four long oak tables joined together with iron clamps. It was twelve feet long and eight feet wide, drawn on three-ply vellum made from the skins of sheep that had grazed on the high pastures before the foundation of the city.

The ink was black, green, red, and blue.

The black lines were roads that had been measured three times by three separate surveyors.

The green lines were parks and gardens—though most of these had been pinched down to small, olive-colored splatters no larger than a postage stamp.

The red lines were public buildings: the High Court, the Mint, the Granary, the Prison.

And the blue lines—the blue lines were the ghosts.

They were drawn in pale ultramarine ink that had been diluted with vinegar so that it would fade after twenty years. The blue lines represented the streets that were in *transition*—the places that were being forgotten, but had not yet completely drawn their shoulders together and vanished into the soil.

I stood over the table with a bottle of blue ink and a fine crow-quill pen.

I found the square marked *The District of the Weavers*.

Threadneedle Street was there, a thin, crooked blue worm crawling between the thick red block of the Steam Loom Works and the black line of the River Sulis.

I dipped my pen.

I ought to have drawn a red cross through Numbers Fourteen through Twenty-Eight. I ought to have taken my razor and scraped away the small blue square that marked Master Vane’s workshop, leaving only the clean, cream-colored surface of the blank vellum to show where the land had become empty and void.

That was the rule. That was the Science of the Third Bureau.

*We do not create,* the oath said. *We only subtract.*

I looked at the blue square of Number Twelve.

I remembered the boxwood shuttle. I remembered the forty-eight picks per inch of blue silk warp and wool weft. I remembered the dry, scratchy sound of Master Vane’s thumb rubbing the polished wood while his floorboards shrank around him like a dying leaf.

I did not scrape the vellum.

Instead, I set my crow-quill down and picked up a tiny camel-hair brush—the kind used by the illuminators who decorated the ornamental borders of the Municipal Charters.

I dipped the tip into the blue ink. Then I dipped it into a saucer of clear water, diluting the blue until it was as pale as the eye of an old weaver.

Very carefully, with a hand that had been trained to measure sixty-fourths of an inch by the feel of a screw-thread, I began to draw.

I did not shrink Threadneedle Street.

I widened it.

I drew three new houses behind Master Vane’s lathe-room. I gave them narrow gardens with pear trees against the stone walls. I drew a small lane—a lane that had never existed on any map since the foundation of the city—leading from the back of the loom-works down to the mud-flats of the river.

I called it *Shuttle Lane*.

I gave it six gas lamps. I gave it a pub called *The Weaver’s Rest*. I gave it a small, stone trough where horses could drink cold river water while their drivers unloaded the crates of raw wool.

As I painted the last faint blue line of the watering trough, I felt a strange, cold vibration in the wood of the drawing table beneath my wrists.

It was not a tremor of the earth. It was a shift in the *tension* of the building.

Somewhere three floors above me, in the long, dark corridors of the High Court, a floorboard gave a loud, dry *CRACK*.

It was the sound of a joist expanding. It was the sound of timber remembering that it had once been forty feet long instead of thirty-six.

I held my breath.

The sound did not repeat. But when I leaned down and brought my nose close to the fresh blue ink on the vellum, the smell of vinegar and iron-gall was gone.

In its place was the smell of damp river mud, wet pear leaves, and the sharp, warm scent of wool grease coming off a newly filled shuttle.

***

### VI. The Threshold

At six in the morning, the night-watchman found me sleeping with my head upon the table, my cheek resting against the western edge of the Great Map.

"Julian," he said, shaking my shoulder with a hand that smelled of plug-tobacco and brass polish. "Wake up, lad. The Director's coming down the stairs."

I sat up, my neck stiff, my mouth tasting of zinc and cold tea.

The blue ink had dried.

*Shuttle Lane* was still there. It did not look like an addition; the pale blue ink had sunk into the old sheepskin, blending with the sixty-year-old lines drawn by long-dead surveyors until you could not tell where the old city ended and my lie began.

I packed my brass tools into my walnut box—the dividers, the leaded silk, the obsidian points, the iron-gall ink.

I did not wait for Director Mara to reach the sub-level. I took the narrow spiral stairs that led up to the delivery yard behind the kitchens, where the coal carts were already backing in through the fog.

The air outside was freezing. A low, river-born mist had crept over the granite walls during the night, wrapping the street lamp posts in thick, yellow scarves of moisture.

I walked north.

I did not take the tram. I did not take the new iron bridge. I walked through the small, twisting alleyways that were not supposed to be there anymore—the ones that had been marked for cancellation five years ago, but somehow still hung on between the backs of the soap factories and the timber yards.

I reached the District of the Weavers at seven.

The fog was so thick here that I could only see ten feet in front of my boots. The silence was absolute—no cart wheels, no milk-bells, no shouting of newsboys.

I turned the corner where Threadneedle Street was supposed to end.

According to my field book from yesterday, I should have found a blank brick wall belonging to the Steam Loom Works, pressed tight against the side of Master Vane’s house.

I did not find a wall.

I found an opening.

It was a narrow lane, paved with rough river cobbles that were bright with wet moss. On the left side stood three small, timber-framed houses with steep gables and north-facing windows. In the garden of the middle house, a pear tree—stunted and gray with river-mist—lifted its bare, crooked branches toward the sky.

A man was standing at the corner beneath a brass gas lamp that flickered with a small, yellow tongue of flame.

He wore a green coat with mended cuffs, and he was holding a brass key that was six inches long.

"You're early, Surveyor," Master Vane said.

He was not carrying his boxwood shuttle. He didn't need to. It was tucked into his waistcoat pocket, its bright brass tip showing above the leather lip like the beak of a small, sleeping bird.

"Where does this lane go?" I asked, my voice soundless in the damp air.

Vane looked down the lane. The fog was beginning to lift, just enough to show the long, gray curve of the cobbles as they dipped down toward the river.

"It goes to the water," he said. "There's a wharf at the end. A small one. Enough for two barges of timber."

"It wasn't here yesterday," I said.

Vane smiled. His teeth were yellow and few, but his eyes were bright—brighter than they had been in his narrow room with the four glass panes.

"It's been here seventy years, Julian," he said. "We just forgot to open the door."

He turned and walked down the lane, his boots making a crisp, heavy *clack-clack-clack* against the cobbles. It was a good sound. It was the sound of a man who weighed one hundred and sixty pounds, walking on stone that had five feet of solid earth beneath it.

I did not follow him.

I set my walnut box down on the curb at the entrance to Shuttle Lane.

I unclasped the brass latches. I took out my field book—the one filled with columns of figures, purple *CANCELLED* stamps, and measurements of rooms that had shrunk to nothing.

I opened it to the first page.

I took my obsidian-tipped dividers and I drove them straight through the thick rag paper, through the leather cover, and deep into the wet wood of the walnut box itself, locking them together in a single, unyielding cross.

Then I left the box sitting on the cobbles beneath the gas lamp.

I walked back toward the city—not by the High Court, not by the Bureau, and not by the great stone avenues that had been measured by iron chains.

I walked through the spaces between the lines.

I found an alley where the gas lamps were out. I found a yard where three old men were playing bowls in the gray light, using wooden balls that had been turned on lathes that were demolished in '92. I found a tea-house that sat in the middle of a street that the Great Map said was six feet wide.

The tea-house was three stories high, and its windows were lit with small, warm tallow candles that smelled of mutton fat and cinnamon.

I went inside.

I sat down at a small marble table near the hearth. The floorboards were pine, seven inches wide, with knots that looked like dark, open eyes.

A girl came to my table. She carried a heavy tin pot and two white stoneware cups.

"Are you the new surveyor?" she asked.

"No," I said, reaching into my coat pocket and finding two copper coins that were so worn they had lost the face of the King. "I am the man who lost the tape measure."

She poured the tea. It was dark, hot, and smelled of wood-smoke.

Outside the window, I heard the sound of the city—not the city of iron and concrete, not the city that shrank every night at four in the morning, but the city that lives under the charcoal drawings of girls with hazel eyes.

It was very wide. It was very long. And as far as I could hear through the clear, winter air, it had no walls at all.
